title: Types of Manufacturing Process
description: The six process types — wasting, shaping, forming, additive, joining, finishing — and how each changes material.
content_html:
What is a Manufacturing Process?

Every engineered product starts as a raw material and ends as a finished component through one or more manufacturing process. The OCR specification groups these operations into six types, and understanding what each type does — and how it changes the material — is the foundation of the whole R041 unit. Each process type is suited to certain materials and certain scales of production, so choosing the right one is a core engineering skill.

Wasting

A wasting process removes material from a workpiece. The material that is cut, drilled, filed or turned away becomes waste — hence the name. The starting block is always larger than the finished part. Common wasting operations include sawing, drilling, filing, turning on a lathe, and milling on a CNC machine. Wasting processes are widely used for metals and plastics, and they can achieve very precise dimensions and smooth surface finishes. The main disadvantage is the waste generated, which adds to material cost and must be disposed of safely.

Key Fact

Wasting processes remove material from a workpiece to achieve the desired shape. The material removed becomes waste swarf or offcuts and cannot be recovered, so careful planning minimises excess material loss.

Shaping

Shaping processes give a material its form by pouring or injecting it into a mould cavity while it is in a liquid or semi-liquid state — the material fills the cavity and solidifies into the desired shape. The material is not removed; instead, it fills the cavity of the mould and solidifies into the desired shape. Sand casting, die casting, and injection moulding are all shaping processes. Shaping is particularly efficient for complex three-dimensional forms because the mould defines every detail in a single operation. It suits metals and polymers and is commonly used in high-volume production.

Shaping uses a fluid or semi-fluid material that takes the shape of a mould cavity — the material has no fixed form before the process begins. Forming, by contrast, starts with a solid workpiece that is deformed plastically by applying force — forging, press forming, vacuum forming and strip heating are all forming processes. In both cases no material is removed, but the mechanism is different: shaping relies on fluidity, forming relies on plasticity. This distinction is commonly tested in the OCR exam.

Forming

Forming processes change the shape of a solid material by applying mechanical force, heat, or both, without removing any material. Forging hammers hot metal into shape; press forming bends sheet metal; vacuum forming stretches a softened thermoplastic sheet over a mould using atmospheric pressure. The material is plastically deformed — meaning the change is permanent. Forming is valued because it generates very little waste and can improve the mechanical properties of metals by aligning the grain structure. It is widely used in the automotive, aerospace and packaging industries.

Key Fact

The six process types are wasting, shaping, forming, additive, joining, and finishing. Only wasting removes material; shaping and forming change its form; additive builds it up; joining combines parts; finishing alters the surface.

Additive Processes

Additive processes build up a product layer by layer from a digital model, adding material only where it is needed. 3D printing using fused deposition modelling (FDM) is the primary additive process on the specification. A thermoplastic filament is melted and deposited in precise layers by a print head that follows a computer-generated path. Additive manufacturing produces virtually no waste, can create complex internal geometries impossible to achieve by wasting, and requires no tooling. It is ideal for prototypes and one-off parts but is currently slower and more costly for large production volumes than traditional methods.

Joining

Joining processes connect two or more components or materials. They can be permanent — such as brazing, MIG/MAG welding, or riveting — or temporary, such as mechanical fastening with nuts and bolts or self-tapping screws. The key characteristic is that joining does not change the form of the individual parts significantly; it combines them into an assembly. Choice of joining method depends on the materials involved, the strength required, whether the joint needs to be dismantled, and the production volume.

Finishing

Finishing processes are applied to the surface of a completed component to improve its appearance, protect it from corrosion or wear, or meet a particular functional requirement. Painting by brush or spray and powder coating are the finishing processes named in the specification. Finishing does not change the overall dimensions of a part to any significant degree — it modifies only the surface. It is usually the final stage in manufacture and is important for both commercial appeal and long-term durability.

Students often call drilling a 'forming' process because it changes the shape of a workpiece — but drilling removes material, so it is wasting. Similarly, injection moulding is shaping (liquid polymer fills a mould), not forming (which requires a solid workpiece and plastic deformation). When answering process-type questions, ask yourself: is material being removed (wasting), poured/injected in liquid form (shaping), deformed as a solid (forming), built up layer by layer (additive), connected to another part (joining), or treated on its surface (finishing)? Apply that checklist and you will select the correct category every time.
exam_tip_html: When an exam question asks you to 'state the type of manufacturing process' used for a given operation, use the exact specification term — wasting, shaping, forming, additive, joining, or finishing. Do not invent hybrid names. For 'explain' questions, add how the process changes the material: for example, 'drilling is a wasting process because it removes material from the workpiece to create a hole, generating waste swarf.' A one-word process type without explanation scores only 1 mark; a type plus a clear mechanism scores full marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The six process types are wasting, shaping, forming, additive, joining, and finishing — each changes material in a distinct way, from removal through to surface treatment.
  • Wasting removes material; shaping and forming change its form without removing it; additive builds up; joining connects components; finishing modifies only the surface.
  • Choosing the correct process type for a manufacturing scenario is a core exam skill — always link your answer to how the chosen process changes the material.

glossary_terms.definition: A controlled operation that changes the form, shape or surface of a raw material to create a useful product or component.
A manufacturing process that removes material from a workpiece to achieve the desired shape, generating waste swarf or offcuts.
A manufacturing process that permanently or temporarily connects two or more separate components or materials.
A process that builds up a product layer by layer from a digital model, adding material only where it is needed.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a wasting process?
A) Injection moulding
B) Vacuum forming
C) Drilling
D) Brazing
State two process types that change the shape of a material without removing any material from the workpiece.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: shaping / forming / additive / joining (accept any two that correctly do not involve material removal). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why drilling a hole in a metal block is classified as a wasting process.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as wasting; 1 mark for stating material is removed from the workpiece; 1 mark for a developed point such as the removed material becomes waste swarf that cannot be recovered, or that the starting block must be larger than the finished part. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by an additive manufacturing process. Give one example of a product that would be suitable for this process.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): a process that builds up a product layer by layer from a digital model, adding material only where it is needed / produces virtually no waste (2 marks for a developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement such as 'it adds material'). Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a prototype engineering component or a custom bracket produced by FDM 3D printing, with a reason why it suits that process — such as complex geometry, one-off production, or no tooling required (2 marks for a specific applied example with justification; 1 mark for naming a product without justification). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A manufacturer needs to produce 10,000 identical plastic housings for an electric motor. The housings have a complex internal cavity.

Discuss which process type or types would be most appropriate for manufacturing the housings at this scale.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two process types, with specific reasoning applied to the scenario. For example: shaping via injection moulding suits high volumes and complex cavities — the mould is expensive but amortised over 10,000 units, giving low unit cost; contrasted with additive manufacturing, which could produce the complex cavity but is far too slow and costly at this volume. A clear recommendation is reached with justification.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least two process types identified with some reasoning linked to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One process type identified with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A design engineer is evaluating whether to use a wasting process or a forming process to manufacture a steel bracket from a solid billet.

Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of each process type for this application, and justify which you would recommend.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation addressing at least two advantages and one disadvantage of each process type, applied to the steel bracket scenario. Wasting advantages: high dimensional precision, smooth surface finish, suits complex shapes; disadvantages: material waste, higher material cost. Forming advantages: no material waste, can improve grain structure and mechanical properties, efficient for high volume; disadvantages: high tooling cost for dies, limited to simpler shapes compared to multi-axis wasting. A substantiated recommendation is reached — for example, forming (forging) is preferable for high-volume production of a safety-critical bracket due to improved grain structure and lower unit cost, but wasting is preferable for a one-off prototype needing tight tolerances.
Secure (5–6 marks): At least two relevant points on each process type with some application to the scenario and an attempted recommendation.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points made but largely one-sided or without a recommendation.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about one process type, no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which process type removes material from a workpiece to achieve the desired shape?
Injection moulding is an example of which process type?
Additive manufacturing builds a product _____ from a digital model, adding material only where it is needed.
A _____ process connects two or more separate components, either permanently or temporarily.
Match each process type to the correct description of how it changes the material.
right: Alters only the surface for protection or appearance
Removes material from the workpiece as swarf or offcuts
Plastically deforms a solid workpiece without removing material

flashcard_questions.q: What are the six types of manufacturing process named in the OCR R041 specification?
flashcard_questions.a: The six types are wasting, shaping, forming, additive, joining, and finishing, each changing material in a distinct way.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a wasting process change the material?
flashcard_questions.a: A wasting process removes material from the workpiece as swarf or offcuts to achieve the desired shape.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a shaping process change the material?
flashcard_questions.a: A shaping process pours or injects a fluid material into a mould cavity, where it solidifies into the desired form.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a forming process change the material?
flashcard_questions.a: A forming process applies force or heat to a solid workpiece, plastically deforming it into a new shape without removing material.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key advantage of additive manufacturing over wasting?
flashcard_questions.a: Additive manufacturing produces virtually no waste because material is deposited only where it is needed, layer by layer.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of a permanent joining process and one example of a temporary joining process.
flashcard_questions.a: MIG welding is a permanent joining process; a nut and bolt assembly is an example of a temporary joining process.

flashcard_questions.q: What do finishing processes change on a manufactured component?
flashcard_questions.a: Finishing processes change only the surface of a component to improve appearance, resist corrosion, or meet a functional requirement.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is drilling classified as a wasting process rather than a forming process?
flashcard_questions.a: Drilling is wasting because it removes material from the workpiece to create the hole, generating waste swarf.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the two finishing processes listed in the OCR R041 specification.
flashcard_questions.a: The two finishing processes in the specification are painting (by brush or spray) and powder coating.

flashcard_questions.q: What feature of forming processes can improve the mechanical properties of metals?
flashcard_questions.a: Forming processes such as forging align the grain structure of the metal, which increases its strength and toughness.

flashcard_questions.q: Which process type is best suited to producing a complex internal geometry that cannot be machined?
flashcard_questions.a: Additive manufacturing is best suited because it builds up the geometry layer by layer with no tooling restrictions.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main disadvantage of wasting processes compared with forming processes?
flashcard_questions.a: The main disadvantage is material waste — the swarf and offcuts removed cannot be recovered, increasing material cost.
